rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, one-season (2013) field experiment with seven automatic scheduling algorithms in a Fuji apple orchard, RCBD with three blocks. Q2: Abstract, Sec 3.1 and Table 2, Fig 7, Sec 3.2 and Conclusions: automatic plant-/weather-based algorithms (TTT, CWSI, WB) applied about 70% less water than conventional practice while stem water potential stayed in the non-stressed range and soil water deficit stayed below MAD; visual observations of tree growth and fruit size reported per treatment; authors state preliminary results support automatic irrigation management of drip-irrigated apples. Q3: Fig 7a (neutron-probe soil water deficit) and Fig 7b (pressure-chamber midday stem water potential) are two independent methods both showing non-stressed trees under the automatic treatments. Q4: Sec 2.3 and Fig 7, soil water content (neutron probe) and stem water potential measured weekly as the intermediate plant/soil water status through which scheduling affects tree performance. Q7: Sec 3.3 and Table 4: regular cleaning/maintenance of IRTs is necessary to keep the plant-based network running; soil-sensor algorithms need site-specific calibration and more sensors to be reliable; WB requires correct ET estimates, known initial soil water and expected application efficiency. Q8: Abstract/Conclusions call results preliminary; Sec 3.2 states no quantitative yield data because of alternate bearing year; Sec 2.4.2 sensors not field-calibrated; Conclusions restrict WB performance to the conditions of the experimental site and defer yield/quality effects to future studies. Q9: Table 2 SE of mean for applied water per treatment; Fig 7 error bars show SE of mean for soil water deficit and stem water potential.
rows.notes: Single orchard, single season, one crop and soil; no farm/district scale. Crop production per se was not quantified (no yield data); the study's production-relevant evidence is plant water status plus qualitative observations of tree growth and fruit size. The review's cited year (2016) matches this paper although its context sentence refers to the 2015 CWSI paper.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment with a SOIL treatment scheduled from Watermark granular-matrix soil water tension sensors with 80/30 kPa dry/wet thresholds. Q2: Sec 3.1 and Table 2: SOIL applied the lowest seasonal water (214 mm), 53% of the neutron-probe reference and 16% of conventional, significantly less than all other treatments. Q4: Fig 6 and Sec 3.1: soil water potential readings from the Watermark sensors monitored every 15 min, showing readings remained within the 0 to -80 kPa threshold band, explaining why irrigation was withheld. Q7: Sec 3.3: to achieve adequate accuracy, a larger number of Watermark sensors, site-specific calibration of individual sensors, or combined use with water-content sensors appears necessary; Sec 3.1: accuracy of the soil feedback is very important. Q8: Sec 2.4.2 and 3.1: sensors used with factory calibration only, one sensor per plot sampling a limited soil volume possibly away from active roots, heterogeneous soil water distribution under drip making representative tension measurements difficult; preliminary single-season evaluation. Q9: Table 2 reports SE of mean for applied water (32 mm for SOIL); Fig 6 shows SE of mean for Watermark readings.
rows.notes: Applied water quantified by one method (logged irrigation depths), so no triangulation. The water reduction is explicitly attributed to under-irrigation rather than efficient scheduling. Single site, season, crop.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3, own field experiment with a Watermark-sensor-based SOIL treatment. Q2: Sec 3.1, 3.2 and Conclusions: field inspections of SOIL and SL+WB plots showed leaf drop, loss of turgidity, reduced shoot and foliage growth, shorter trees and abnormally small fruit that never ripened, attributed to under-irrigation by the soil-sensor algorithm. Q4: Table 2 and Fig 6: applied irrigation depth and soil water tension in the SOIL plots were measured, documenting the under-irrigation pathway. Q7: Sec 3.3: site-specific calibration, more sensors per plot or combined tension/content sensing stated as necessary for soil-sensor scheduling to deliver enough water. Q8: Sec 3.2: no quantitative fruit yield data collected because trees were in an alternate bearing year; Sec 2.4.2 and 3.1: uncalibrated sensors, one sensor per plot, limited sampled soil volume; stem water potential and neutron probe were not measured in SOIL plots; preliminary one-season study.
rows.notes: The stress and fruit-quality harm rests on visual field observations only; the Watermark readings themselves showed no stress, so the result is not triangulated and no dispersion measure applies to it. Fruit quality was not measured quantitatively.

notes: Full text available. Preliminary one-season (2013) study at one research orchard near Prosser, WA; seven automatic scheduling algorithms compared mainly on applied water, soil/plant water status, cost and simplicity; no yield data.
